title: Camp Stipend Forgery
subject: Criminal Law & Procedure
stem:
Daniel, a former volunteer at a Christian summer-camp, found Stephen's checkbook in the parking lot during a Saturday clean-up day at the camp. The checkbook contained unused (blank) personal checks. Daniel wrote a check on one of those checks payable to "cash" for $750, signed Stephen's name without Stephen's authority, and planned to cash it at a check-cashing store before the camp week ended.

Has Daniel committed forgery?

choices.A: Yes, because Daniel falsely made a check with apparent legal efficacy intending to defraud.
choices.B: No, because Stephen did not actually lose money yet.
choices.C: Yes, but only if Daniel successfully cashes the check.
choices.D: No, because checks are not writings with legal significance.

rightExplanation:
Daniel has committed forgery. He falsely made a check payable to "cash" for $750, signed Stephen's name without authority, and intended to use the check to obtain money he was not owed. A completed check purporting to draw funds on a depositor's account has apparent legal efficacy because, if presented and honored, it would operate to transfer funds from the named account to the holder. Gold Key: forgery is complete when the defendant falsely makes a writing with apparent legal efficacy with intent to defraud; the victim need not actually lose money, and the forger need not successfully utter the document. The "false making" is the actus reus.

Silver Key: when the call asks "has the defendant committed forgery," ask whether the false making has occurred. Loss and successful uttering are not elements of forgery.

c3.label: D (no legal significance)
c3.text: is a tiered_absolute overclaim. The defect is detectable from the answer text: "checks are not writings with legal significance" is a flat absolute. A C3 student trained on overclaim detection can flag it; the Gold Key (apparent legal efficacy) supplies the resolution.

c3.label: C (needs successful uttering)
c3.text: is a wrong-element cut. The element "successful uttering" is not the actus reus of forgery; the false making is. A C3 student trained on actus reus / wrong-element detection can flag it; the Silver Key supplies the resolution.

c3.label: B (no actual loss)
c3.text: is the dominant trap. The defect is intuitive ("no harm, no foul") but the resolution requires the Gold Key: loss is not an element of forgery. The cut is not visible from the C3 frame alone.

c3.label: CLASH
c3.text: C and D are eliminated on overclaim and wrong-element cuts. B and A remain. The axis is "the forgery is not yet complete" (B) vs. "the false making is complete" (A). Both are intuitable framings; the student must name which is correct.

c3.label: CALL
c3.text: The Gold Key resolves the axis: false making is the actus reus of forgery. Loss and successful uttering are not elements. Apply the Gold Key → A.

studentScript: The call asks whether Daniel committed forgery. Cut D: 'checks are not writings with legal significance' is a tiered-absolute overclaim; checks have apparent legal efficacy. Cut C: 'only if Daniel successfully cashes the check' is a wrong-element trap; forgery is complete at the false making, not at the uttering. The remaining tension: 'no actual loss = no forgery' (B) vs. 'false making with intent' (A). Apply the Gold Key: the victim's actual loss is not an element of forgery; the false making is the actus reus. Choose A.

A.signal: After the three distractors are cut, the residual is the false-making answer.
A.lawyer: Forgery is complete at the false making of a writing with apparent legal efficacy with intent to defraud. Model Penal Code § 241.1; common-law forgery rule.

B.signal: The student reaches for 'no harm, no foul.' The defect is the Gold Key: actual loss is not an element of forgery.
B.lawyer: The actus reus of forgery is the false making with intent; the victim's actual loss is not an element. Model Penal Code § 241.1 (purpose to defraud or knowledge of facilitating a fraud); common-law 'apparent legal efficacy' test.

C.signal: The student reads 'plans to cash' as a half-step. The defect is the Silver Key: false making is the actus reus; uttering is a separate crime.
C.lawyer: Forgery is complete at the false making. Uttering a forged instrument is a separate crime, but it is not a required element of forgery itself.

D.signal: The student flags the absolute. The defect is the Gold Key: a check is precisely the writing the forgery rule covers because a check has apparent legal efficacy.
D.lawyer: A check payable to 'cash' that purports to draw on a depositor's account has apparent legal efficacy because, if presented and honored, it would operate to transfer funds. The 'apparent legal efficacy' requirement is the modern common-law test for forgery.

goldKeys.statement: Forgery is complete when the defendant falsely makes a writing with apparent legal efficacy with intent to defraud; the victim need not actually lose money, and the forger need not successfully utter the document. The 'false making' is the actus reus.
goldKeys.trigger: writing falsely made and signed without authority with intent to defraud
goldKeys.unlocks: dominant trap - 'no actual loss = no forgery'
goldKeys.authority: Model Penal Code Section 241.1; common-law forgery (apparent legal efficacy test); state forgery statutes tracking the same elements

remediation.title: Forgery - false making is the actus reus
remediation.signal: A finder of unused checks fills in a check, signs the owner's name without authority, and plans to cash it. The owner has not actually lost money, and the check has not been cashed.
remediation.studentMove: Cut tiered-absolute overclaims (checks have apparent legal efficacy) and wrong-element traps (uttering is not the actus reus of forgery). Then apply the Gold Key: the victim's actual loss is not an element of forgery; the false making is the actus reus.
remediation.tinyRule: Forgery is complete at the false making of a writing with apparent legal efficacy and intent to defraud; loss and successful uttering are not elements.
remediation.trap: The lay intuition 'no harm, no foul' is wrong. The victim need not actually lose money, and the forger need not successfully utter the document.
